Contagious bacterial disease, historically called consumption, usually caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It often infects the [[Lung|lungs]] first but can spread to the kidneys, spine, brain, and other organs. Most infections cause no symptoms and are termed latent, in which case they are not contagious. A small proportion progress to active disease, which can be fatal if untreated. Typical symptoms are chronic cough with blood-containing mucus, fever, night sweats, and weight loss.

The disease spreads through the air when people with active TB in their lungs cough, spit, speak, or sneeze. Latent infection is more likely to become active in people with weakened [[Immune system|immune systems]]. An estimated 5% to 15% of untreated latent cases progress to active TB. Active disease involves the lungs in about 90% of cases; in 15–20% the infection spreads outside them, and in more than 50% of active cases in people with [[HIV]].

Prevention involves screening those at high risk, early detection and treatment, and vaccination with the bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) [[Vaccine|vaccine]]. Treatment requires multiple [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] over a long period; drug-susceptible TB is typically treated with a six-month regimen including isoniazid and rifampicin. Since the 1980s, antibiotic resistance has produced more multidrug-resistant TB.

Latent TB is estimated to affect one-quarter of the world's population, approximately 2 billion people. In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million new cases and 1.23 million deaths made it the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. In the 1800s it caused an estimated quarter of all deaths in Europe. [[Robert Koch]] identified the bacterium in 1882.

Country mainly in [[Anatolia]] in West Asia, with a smaller part, East Thrace, in Southeast Europe. Officially the Republic of Türkiye, it covers 783,562 sq km and has over 86 million people. It borders the Black Sea, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Iraq, Syria, the Mediterranean and Aegean seas, Greece, and Bulgaria. Most inhabitants are ethnic Turks; [[Kurds]] are the largest minority. The state is officially secular; the population is Muslim-majority. [[Ankara]] is the capital; [[Istanbul]] is the largest city and economic center.

Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century, and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243. From 1299 the Ottomans united the Turkish principalities, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The [[Ottoman Empire]] became a global power under Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent, then declined from 1789 onward. It entered World War I in 1914; during the war its government committed genocides against Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian subjects. After defeat, the [[Turkish War of Independence]] abolished the sultanate and led to the Treaty of Lausanne. The republic was proclaimed on October 29, 1923, under its founder and first president, [[Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]]. Turkey remained neutral during most of World War II, fought in the Korean War, and joined [[NATO]] in 1952.

Turkey is a unitary presidential republic and an upper-middle-income emerging economy, ranked 16th by nominal and 11th by PPP-adjusted GDP. It is a founding member of the OECD and G20 and an EU candidate. Its terrain includes coastal plains, a high central plateau, and mountains rising eastward, and earthquakes are frequent.

Country in Northwestern Europe comprising England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland (pop., 2025: over 69 million). Officially the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, it is also called the UK or Britain. It covers 244,376 sq km, including the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of Ireland, and most smaller islands of the [[British Isles]], and shares a land border with the [[Republic of Ireland]]. The capital is [[London]]; Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast are the national capitals of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

The Roman conquest began in AD 43, Anglo-Saxon settlement around 450, and the [[Normans|Norman]] conquest of England in 1066. In 1707 England and Scotland united to form the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]]. The Acts of Union 1800 incorporated the Kingdom of Ireland, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in 1801. Most of Ireland seceded in 1922, and the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927 created the present state.

Britain was the first industrialized country, in the 18th century, and the foremost world power for most of the 19th and early 20th centuries, notably during the Pax Britannica of 1815–1914. At its height in the 1920s the [[British Empire]] encompassed around a quarter of the world's landmass and population. Decolonization led to the independence of most colonies, many of which joined the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

The UK is a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] and parliamentary democracy with three jurisdictions: England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own governments and parliaments with devolved powers. It is a developed country with an advanced economy and nuclear weapons. "Great Britain" conventionally means the island, or England, Scotland, and Wales together.

International intergovernmental organization for maintaining peace and security. Its Charter was signed on June 26, 1945, and entered into force on October 24, 1945. With 193 member states, it is the largest international organization; the Holy See and the State of Palestine are observer states.

The UN is headquartered in [[New York City]], with other major offices at Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna, and The Hague. It has six principal organs: the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council, [[International Court of Justice]], and Secretariat. Together with specialized agencies such as the [[World Health Organization]], they form the UN System. It operates 11 peacekeeping missions and has deployed over 70 since 1948, receiving the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988. It has focused on economic and social development, particularly during the wave of [[Decolonization|decolonization]] in the mid-20th century.

Its predecessor, the [[League of Nations]], came into being on January 10, 1920, after World War I leaders including U.S. President [[Woodrow Wilson]] advocated a world body. The League effectively closed down when World War II began in 1939. [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] coined the term "United Nations" for the Allied countries, and the Declaration by United Nations was signed on January 1, 1942, by the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, and China, and by 22 other nations the next day.

Critics cite perceived ineffectiveness, bias, and corruption, including the Oil-for-Food scandal. They also note that vetoes by permanent Security Council members (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States) have blocked resolutions on conflicts such as those in Syria and Ukraine. Supporters credit it with aiding decolonization and coordinating responses to health crises.

Federal republic primarily in North America, consisting of 50 states and a federal capital district, [[Washington, D.C.]] The 48 contiguous states border Canada and Mexico, with [[Alaska]] in the northwest and the archipelago of [[Hawaii]] in the Pacific. It has the world's fourth-largest total area, 9,833,517 sq km, and third-largest population, exceeding 341 million.

Paleo-Indians migrated from North Asia to North America at least 15,000 years ago. British colonization beginning in 1607 established the [[Thirteen Colonies]]. Disputes over taxation without parliamentary representation sparked the [[American Revolution]]; independence was formally declared in the Lee Resolution of July 2, 1776, two days before the Declaration of Independence, and the 1775–1783 Revolutionary War confirmed international recognition. The Constitution dates from 1787. The country expanded westward through purchase, settlement, and conquest of European- and Indigenous-controlled territory. A sectional division over slavery led 11 Southern states to secede and form the [[Confederate States of America]], fighting the Union in the Civil War of 1861–1865; slavery was abolished with Union victory. By 1900 the U.S. had emerged as a great power. It entered World War II after Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, then rivaled the Soviet Union in the [[Cold War]]; the Soviet collapse in 1991 left it the sole superpower.

The Constitution established a separation of powers among legislative, executive, and judicial branches. Executive authority is vested in a president; Congress is bicameral, composed of the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Supreme Court exercises judicial review, and federalism grants the 50 states substantial autonomy.

The economy accounts for over a quarter of nominal global GDP and has been the world's largest since about 1890; wealth inequality is highly pronounced. The U.S. makes up nearly a third of global military spending. "America" derives from the first name of Amerigo Vespucci and was first used as a place name in 1507.

Totality of space, time, matter, and energy, with all the structures they form, from subatomic particles to galactic filaments. The word comes from Latin *universus*, "combined into one"; Greek philosophers from Pythagoras onward called it *to pan* ("the all") and *kosmos*.

[[Cosmology]] has established that the universe has been expanding and cooling for 13.8 billion years since the [[Big Bang]], an age inferred by fitting cosmological models to precision data, especially measurements of the [[Cosmic microwave background|cosmic microwave background]]. The [[Observable universe|observable portion]] is approximately 93 billion light-years in diameter; it is bounded by cosmological horizons, and the total size is not known. Early cosmological models were geocentric; astronomical observations during the Scientific Revolution led to a heliocentric model. The Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the [[Milky Way]], which is one of a few hundred billion galaxies in the observable universe. At the largest scale, galaxies are distributed uniformly; at smaller scales they form clusters and superclusters, arranged in filaments around voids in a foam-like structure. General relativity and discoveries of the early 20th century led to the modern view of an expanding universe.

In the Big Bang model, the earliest state was extremely hot and dense. An intense period of expansion called [[Cosmic inflation|cosmic inflation]] is postulated to explain many observations, though much of the earliest time is not understood. Big Bang nucleosynthesis lasted about 15 minutes and produced helium, small amounts of deuterium, and traces of lithium. After about 377,000 years, electrons and nuclei formed the first stable atoms, and the universe became transparent;  the photons released still form that background radiation. Matter's energy density overtook that of photons and neutrinos at around 47,000 years. The first stars formed after around 100–300 million years and gradually reionized the universe, seeding it with elements heavier than helium. After about 9.8 billion years the density of matter fell below that of [[Dark energy|dark energy]], beginning the present era, in which expansion accelerates.

In the widely accepted ΛCDM model, [[Dark matter|dark matter]] accounts for about 25.8%±1.1% of the mass and energy in the universe, dark energy about 69.2%±1.2%, and ordinary baryonic matter only 4.84%±0.1%; stars, planets, and visible gas clouds form about 6% of that ordinary matter. The nature of dark energy remains unknown. Competing hypotheses exist about the ultimate fate of the universe and what, if anything, preceded the Big Bang.

Institution of [[Tertiary education|tertiary education]] and research that awards [[Academic degree|academic degrees]] in several disciplines. The word derives from [[Latin]] *universitas magistrorum et scholarium*, roughly "community of teachers and scholars". Universities typically offer undergraduate and postgraduate programs.

The first universities developed in Europe from schools maintained by the Church to educate priests. The oldest shared several features: they used the word *universitas*, drew students from beyond the local region, taught at least one higher faculty (theology, law, or medicine) beyond the seven liberal arts, awarded degrees through a public oral event managed by a guild of masters, had some autonomy from ecclesiastical authorities, enjoyed academic freedom, and issued secular as well as religious degrees. The oldest by these criteria are the [[University of Bologna]] (established around 1088), Paris, [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]], and Palencia.

Academic freedom is traced to Bologna's charter, the Constitutio Habita, of 1155 or 1158, which guaranteed traveling scholars unhindered passage. On September 18, 1988, 430 rectors signed the Magna Charta Universitatum. Debate continues over whether academic freedom at publicly funded universities should support public goods such as social justice or also include a prerogative to pursue knowledge for its own sake.

Earlier centers of learning existed. Theodosius II founded the Pandidakterion, later the University of Constantinople, in 425. Nalanda was founded around 427 by Kumaragupta I of the [[Gupta Empire]] and attracted scholars such as [[Xuanzang]]; it was destroyed in 1202, and scholars dispute calling it a university in the modern sense. Cathedral schools arose across France and Germany, and monastic schools flourished in the 9th and 10th centuries.

Seventh planet from the [[Sun]], a cyan-colored [[Giant planet|ice giant]]. Most of it consists of water, ammonia, and [[Methane|methane]] in a supercritical phase that astronomers call "ice". Its diameter is about 51,118 km, third-largest among the Solar System's planets, and its mass is fourth-largest. A rocky core lies inside a volatile mantle, surrounded by a thick hydrogen and helium atmosphere. The atmosphere has the lowest minimum temperature of any planet, 49 K (−224 °C), and peak winds of 900 km/h. Internal heat is very low compared with other giant planets, for reasons that remain unclear.

Uranus has an axial tilt of 82.23° and a retrograde rotation period of 17 hours and 14 minutes. Over its 84-Earth-year orbit, each pole receives about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness. Its [[Magnetic field|magnetic field]] is highly asymmetric. The extremely dark ring system reflects only about 2% of incoming light. The planet has 29 [[Natural satellite|natural satellites]], including five major moons: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon.

Visible to the naked eye, Uranus was never recognized as a planet by ancient observers because of its dimness and slow motion. It was apparently observed by [[Hipparchus]] in 128 BC, and John Flamsteed cataloged it as 34 Tauri in 1690. [[William Herschel]] observed it on March 13, 1781, from Bath, England, and first reported it as a comet. It was the first planet found with the aid of a telescope, and its discovery effectively doubled the size of the known Solar System. About seven decades later, consensus was reached to name it after the Greek god Ouranos.

[[Voyager 2]] flew past in 1986, the only visit so far. The 2023–2032 Planetary Science Decadal Survey made a proposed Uranus Orbiter and Probe a top priority.

Process of population shift from [[Rural area|rural]] to urban areas, in which human settlements form and grow as more people live and work in cities and towns. The term refers to the proportion of a national population living in areas classified as urban, rather than the absolute number of urban residents. It is studied in disciplines including [[Urban planning|urban planning]], geography, sociology, and economics.

Until the 18th century, most people engaged in subsistence agriculture, and towns were small centers of trade and small-scale manufacture, keeping the rural-to-urban ratio at a fixed equilibrium. The British Agricultural Revolution and the [[Industrial Revolution]] of the late 18th century broke this balance. In England and Wales, the share of the population living in cities of more than 20,000 people rose from 17% in 1801 to 54% in 1891. Under a broader definition, the urbanized share in 1891 was 72% in England and Wales, 37% in France, 41% in Prussia, and 28% in the United States. Laborers converged on industrial cities such as [[Manchester]] and [[Birmingham]], and [[Public transport|public transport]] let cities expand outward. Urbanization spread across the Western world and, since the 1950s, the developing world. About 15% of the world's population lived in cities at the turn of the 20th century. According to the [[United Nations|UN]], more than 50% did by 2007, for the first time in history.

The global urban share rose from about 3% in 1800 to 58% in 2025 under national definitions, or 81% under the UN Degree of Urbanization method, covering about 4.8 billion people. Mechanization of agriculture and the pull of higher wages and amenities drive the shift, which correlates strongly with economic development. It brings pressures such as air pollution, resource strain, and informal settlements, especially in low-income countries, while offering opportunities for more efficient use of resources and land. The UN's 2025 World Urbanization Prospects project that city and town dwellers will make up 83% of the world population by 2050, mostly in Asia and Africa.

Biological preparation that provides active acquired immunity to a particular infectious or malignant disease. A vaccine typically contains an agent resembling a disease-causing microorganism, often made from weakened or killed forms of the microbe, its toxins, or one of its surface proteins. The agent stimulates the [[Immune system|immune system]] to recognize and destroy it, and to recognize and destroy associated microorganisms encountered in the future. Vaccines can be prophylactic, preventing future infection, or therapeutic, fighting an existing disease such as cancer. Giving a vaccine is called [[Vaccination|vaccination]]; the science of developing and producing them is vaccinology.

Inoculation against [[Smallpox|smallpox]] was first recorded in 16th-century China, with earlier hints in the 10th century, and was brought from Turkey to Britain in 1721 by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. In 1796, [[Edward Jenner]] showed that exposure to cowpox protected against smallpox. The terms "vaccine" and "vaccination" come from *Variolae vaccinae* ("smallpox of the cow"), the phrase Jenner used in 1798. In 1881 [[Louis Pasteur]] proposed extending the terms to the new protective inoculations.

Vaccination is widely regarded as the most effective method of preventing infectious diseases. It is largely responsible for the eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980, and the restriction of polio, [[Measles|measles]], and tetanus from much of the world. The [[World Health Organization]] reports licensed vaccines for twenty-five preventable infections. Routine childhood immunizations are credited with preventing an estimated 154 million deaths since 1974. In the United States, measles cases fell from 763,094 in 1958, with 552 deaths, to fewer than 150 per year after vaccines were introduced.

Limitations exist. A lack of response occurs in an estimated 2–10% of individuals, and adaptive immunity can take 1–2 weeks to develop. Adverse events are usually mild, such as injection-site pain and fever; rare serious outcomes include anaphylaxis (about 1.3 per million doses). The scientific consensus is that vaccines are safe and effective, but policy mandates, concerns about adjuvants, and long-term safety fuel debate and [[Vaccine hesitancy|vaccine hesitancy]].
